Figure 1. Representatives of natural bisanthraquinones dimerized via

figure_candidates.label: Figure 2
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 2. Identiﬁcation of the rug gene cluster governing the
biosynthesis of skyrin (1) and rugulosin A (2). (A) rug gene cluster
organization in Talaromyces sp. YE3016. (B) HPLC proﬁlings for 1
and/or 2 produced by the wild-type (WT) and mutant strains
(ΔrugA−ΔrugH). The chromatograms were recorded at 360 nm.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 3
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 3. Expression of the rug cluster in Aspergillus oryzae (AO).
HPLC proﬁles of the EtOAc extracts derived from the transformants
harboring one (i, rugA), two (ii, rugAB), three (iii, rugABE), four (iv,
rugABEF), ﬁve (v, rugABEFG; vi, rugABEFH), and six genes (vii,
rugABEFGH), respectively. The chromatograms were recorded at 360
nm in comparison with the authentic materials of skyrin (1) and
rugulosin A (2). The mutant-formed products (3 and 5−9) were
characterized by isolation and spectral interpretation of pure
compounds.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 4. Functional characterization and substrate promiscuity of
RugG. (A) HPLC proﬁlings at 360 nm for bisanthraquinone products
that might form upon the emodin (5)-exposed culture of Aspergillus
oryzae (AO) or Saccharomyces cerevisiae RC01 (SC-RC01) trans-
formants carrying diﬀerent genes: (i) empty AO; (ii) AO with rugG
(AO-rugG); (iii) empty SC-RC01; (iv) SC-RC01 with rugG (SC-
RC01-rugG); (v) authentic standards of skyrin (1), rugulosin A (2),
and 9. (B) Substrate-dependent RugG-catalyzed dimerization pattern.
The structural diﬀerence of substrate candidates from 5 is drawn in
red. The SC-RC01-rugG transformant was cultivated on exposure to
one or two substrates, and the products that were generated were
evidenced from the LC-UV-MS analysis according to the molecular
weights of anticipated bisanthraquinones and the red-shifts displayed
in UV spectra owing to the aryl-extended conjugation system (Figures
S14−S20). aYield determined by LC-MS analysis. bNo reaction.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Figure 5. Functional characterization of RugH. (A and B) HPLC proﬁlings of the EtOAc extracts from the skyrin (1)-exposed cultures of
Aspergillus oryzae (AO)-rugH (A, i) and Saccharomyces cerevisiae (SC)-BJ5464-rugH (B, i), from the emodin (5)-supplemented cultivations of AO-
rugH (A, ii) and SC-BJ5464-rugH (B, ii), from the 5-exposed cocultures of AO-rugG with AO-rugH (A, iii) and of SC-RC01-rugG with SC-BJ5464-
rugH (B, iii), and from the 5-supplemented cultures of AO-rugGH (A, iv) and SC-RC01-rugGH (B, iv) transformants, in comparison with authentic
samples of 1, 2, and 5 (v). (C) Conserved catalytic tetrad in the structure model of RugH. The structure model of RugH complexed with NADPH
was generated by the I-TASSER server. The overall structure of the RugH-NADPH complex is shown as a cartoon. The tetrad (D52, Y57, K81, and
H117) is shown as sticks, and NADPH as sticks and balls. (D) HPLC proﬁlings of the methanol extract of the fungal hyphae from the emodin (5)-
exposed culture of AO-rugGH cotransformants with mutation at the conserved catalytic tetrad residues of RugH.
